scrutinized all 11 cases individually for filler/tautology: none is `expect(true).toBe(true)` or existence-only. Status-401/500 cases assert both kind AND a message-substring computed from the actual input, not a constant. The string-status ('500') case is grounded in the plan's own Task 1 ACTION prose, which literally says 'an object carrying a numeric status field' (grepped and confirmed at plan lines 279, 56, 93, 172, 362, 461, 516) -- this is a real, plan-specified contract (typeof status === 'number'), not an invented requirement test-writer added unilaterally; ApiError's own class field is typed `status: number`, so the classifier duck-typing on a string status would silently misclassify a non-ApiError third-party error shape carrying a string status, which the plan's structural-typing design explicitly guards against. The null/undefined/string-primitive cases are not filler: classifyRequestFailure(cause: unknown) is invoked from a catch block that can catch any thrown value including non-Error primitives (valid in JS), and the `not.toThrow()` assertions are meaningful because a naive unguarded `cause.status` property access on null/undefined throws a TypeError -- this is exactly the defensive-programming class of bug these cases catch, not decoration. The generic-Error-with-no-status case genuinely guards against an instanceof-TypeError-keyed implementation: the plan's own MDN citation names TypeError specifically as fetch()'s rejection type, which is precisely what could tempt an instanceof-based (rather than structural status-field) implementation the plan explicitly rejects.

scrutinized pairwise, specifically the two cases the dispatch flagged: (1) the 401/500 individual cases (each asserts kind + message-contains-status-number for ONE input) and the cross-status distinctness case (asserts message(401) !== message(500), a genuinely different observable property -- output-to-output inequality, not input-to-property containment) are not a literal duplicate; constructed the counter-example that shows non-redundancy -- a constant message string that happens to embed both possible status substrings (e.g. 'Error 401 or 500 occurred') would pass the two individual containment checks yet fail the distinctness check, so the distinctness case has real, independent catching power the individual cases lack. (2) the cross-kind distinctness case (server-unreachable message !== http-error message) is not redundant with the per-case `.kind` checks either: `.kind` is an internal tag never rendered to the UI (`handleFailure` only surfaces `.message` into `error` state), so message-level distinctness across kinds is the only test that actually verifies AC-A2's real 'visibly distinct' requirement, which is a message-level, not kind-level, contract. (3) the three no-status boundary/network-unreachable inputs (bare {} object, non-object string primitive 'boom', null/undefined) are distinct equivalence classes for a property-access implementation: {} is a property-less object baseline, 'boom' is a non-object primitive that still permits harmless `.status` access (returns undefined, no throw), and null/undefined are the only inputs where naive `.status` access actually throws -- these are not interchangeable inputs. No duplicate pair found across all 11 cases.
